explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "you without money, come, buy, and eat!" (Isaiah 55:1). Empty pockets, and you're still invited. I've never seen a sale where a bare wallet gets you through the door, but this one is God's.

Nice try, friend, but there's no side hustle in this verse. The LORD says, "you without money, come, buy, and eat!" (Isaiah 55:1). He tells them to come, with nothing about earning first. The only thing they need to bring is themselves.

Friend, I get why you'd picture a velvet rope and a guy with a clipboard. But the LORD never mentions a gate. He says, "you without money, come, buy, and eat!" (Isaiah 55:1). Come means come in, not hang around outside.

Close, baker, but this one flips it around. The LORD asks, "Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?" (Isaiah 55:2). So the labor goes to something that does NOT satisfy. The question is a warning, not a compliment.

You got it, baker. The LORD asks, "Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?" (Isaiah 55:2). Hard work poured into something that leaves you empty. I've pressed a lot of cookies, and I'd hate for all that effort to leave nobody full.

Right on, friend. The LORD says, "Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in the richest of foods" (Isaiah 55:2). Listening comes first, and the good eating follows. Even I know you hear the oven timer BEFORE you pull the tray.
Not this time, baker. The LORD has just asked why they spend money on what is not bread. His answer isn't to save it. He says, "Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good" (Isaiah 55:2).

I know that feeling, friend. Just push harder, right? But the LORD has just asked about labor spent on what does not satisfy. His answer is, "Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good" (Isaiah 55:2). He doesn't ask for more sweat.

That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "My loving devotion promised to David" (Isaiah 55:3). David was Israel's king. That's a promise with a long history behind it, and God is putting it in front of everybody here.

Good name, friend, and Moses, Israel's leader, matters a lot in the Bible. But this verse names someone else. The LORD says, "My loving devotion promised to David" (Isaiah 55:3). David was Israel's king.

I see why you went there, baker. Abraham is the man God promised a great nation (Genesis 12:2). But in this verse the LORD names someone else: "My loving devotion promised to David" (Isaiah 55:3). David was Israel's king.

Careful, friend, this one went the other way. The LORD says, "nations who do not know you will run to you" (Isaiah 55:5). Nobody is turning away. They're RUNNING toward you. It's like a line out the door of a bakery, except this one is nations.

You caught it, baker. The LORD says, "nations who do not know you will run to you" (Isaiah 55:5). They don't know you, and they run to you anyway. That's a lot of cardio for people who have never met.

That's right, baker. The verse ends, "For the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, has bestowed glory on you." (Isaiah 55:5). That "For" gives the reason. The glory comes from the LORD, and the nations run because of it.

Almost, friend, but the verse does give a reason. It says, "For the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, has bestowed glory on you." (Isaiah 55:5). That "For" points straight at the glory. It's a gift from the LORD, and I'd have a hard time giving a gift like that.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "Let the wicked man forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts" (Isaiah 55:7). Then comes the good part: let him return to the LORD. The door is open for the wicked man to turn around and walk back.

Good guess, friend, but the rich man doesn't show up in this verse. It says, "Let the wicked man forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts" (Isaiah 55:7). So it's the wicked man who's told to turn back. Money isn't what this verse is about.

Not quite, baker. This verse doesn't mention a foreign man at all. It says, "Let the wicked man forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts" (Isaiah 55:7). The wicked man is the one told to forsake his way.

Perfect, friend. The verse says, "for He will freely pardon" (Isaiah 55:7). Freely means no catch and no haggling. When I think of everything I ever got wrong in a kitchen, that word sounds mighty good.
Nope, baker, nobody's waiting on hold for this one. The verse says, "for He will freely pardon" (Isaiah 55:7). Freely is the word. It's a pardon that's offered with open hands.
I know it sounds like how the world works, friend. A little here, a little there, and then a catch. But the verse says, "for He will freely pardon" (Isaiah 55:7). Freely, with no asterisk.

I get the slip, baker, but the LORD says the opposite. He declares, "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways" (Isaiah 55:8). His are not the same as ours. I've been wrong about a recipe before. He isn't wrong about anything.

That's it, friend. The LORD declares, "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways" (Isaiah 55:8). His thoughts and ways are not ours. It's a good reminder that I don't have to figure out everything before I trust Him.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts" (Isaiah 55:9). Look up at a night sky and try to reach it. That's how far it is.

Good picture, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. The LORD says, "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts" (Isaiah 55:9). The heavens are much higher than any mountain. I'd say that's quite a gap.

Nice try, baker, but the verse picks something else. The LORD says, "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts" (Isaiah 55:9). It's the heavens above the earth. That's about as high as it gets.

That's right, baker. The verse says rain and snow "fall from heaven and do not return without watering the earth" (Isaiah 55:10). It comes down, and the ground gets watered. Then it makes things bud and sprout, and gives seed to sow and food to eat.

Not this time, friend. The verse says rain and snow "fall from heaven and do not return without watering the earth" (Isaiah 55:10). They don't go back until the earth is watered. The job gets done first.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty" (Isaiah 55:11). Just like the rain, it comes back with the job done. When God sends His word, it doesn't come back with nothing to show.

Good word, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. The LORD says, "My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty" (Isaiah 55:11). Empty is the word. It means His word does what He sends it to do.

Sweet thought, baker, but the verse says something else. The LORD says, "My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty" (Isaiah 55:11). Empty is the word. His word never comes back with nothing done.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "the mountains and hills will burst into song before you" (Isaiah 55:12). Mountains, singing. I can't even carry a tune in the shower, and I'm a stamper with a mustache.
That's a good picture, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, "the mountains and hills will burst into song before you" (Isaiah 55:12). It's a song, not a bow. It's a celebration.

That one sounds dramatic, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, "the mountains and hills will burst into song before you" (Isaiah 55:12). The hills sing while you go out with joy. It's a happy scene.

Perfect, baker. The verse calls it "an everlasting sign, never to be destroyed" (Isaiah 55:13). Everlasting means it keeps going. Most things I make get eaten by dinner, so that's a different kind of lasting.

explanations.answer: A sign that fades in time
explanations.explanation: I understand, friend, since most signs fade, like old paint on a bakery window. But this verse says the opposite. It calls it "an everlasting sign, never to be destroyed" (Isaiah 55:13). It doesn't fade.

Good guess, baker, but the verse doesn't say that. It says all this "will make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign, never to be destroyed" (Isaiah 55:13). The sign is everlasting, and it's for the LORD's name. Nothing in the verse limits it to one nation.
